ABSTRACT: The Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) is a planetary-scale convective system char-
acterized by large-scale envelopes of enhanced and suppressed convection that contain numerous
mesoscale convective systems (MCSs). While MCSs are widely recognized as the fundamental
convective elements embedded within the MJO, their relationship with the MJO is intrinsically
two-way: the MJO modulates the large-scale dynamical and thermodynamic environment that
organizes MCS activity, while the collective upscale impacts of MCSs feed back onto the MJO
through the transport of momentum and heat. However, the nature of this bidirectional interaction
remains insufficiently quantified from an observational perspective. In this study, we use satellite-
based MJO indices together with a long-term, objectively tracked MCS dataset to investigate the
two-way feedback mechanisms between the MJO and MCSs. By compositing MCS activity across
different MJO phases and analyzing their environmental conditions, we quantify how the evolving
MJO circulation regulates MCS frequency, intensity, and organization. At the same time, we
diagnose the aggregate influence of MCS populations on the large-scale MJO circulation through
their associated momentum and thermodynamic anomalies. Our results reveal a robust two-way
coupling between the MJO and MCSs. Enhanced MCS activity preferentially occurs in specific
MJO phases associated with favorable moisture, instability, and vertical shear, indicating strong
MJO control on MCS organization. Conversely, periods of enhanced MCS activity are associated
with coherent large-scale circulation anomalies consistent with upscale transport of momentum
and moisture that reinforce the MJO convective envelope and support its eastward propagation.
This feedback suggests that MCSs are not merely passive responses to the MJO environment, but
actively contribute to its maintenance and evolution. These findings highlight the importance of
treating the MJO–MCS relationship as a coupled, two-way interaction across scales, providing
an observational basis for understanding how mesoscale convective organization contributes to
intraseasonal variability in the tropics.

SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT:
The Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) strongly influences
global weather and climate variability, yet current understanding of how it interacts with embedded
mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) remains incomplete. Using long-term satellite-based MJO
indices and objectively tracked MCS data, this study quantifies the two-way feedback between
the MJO and MCSs from observations. We show that the MJO systematically organizes MCS
activity through large-scale moisture, instability, and wind shear conditions, while aggregated
MCS activity in turn feeds back onto the MJO circulation through coherent large-scale anomalies
consistent with upscale transport processes. These results demonstrate that MCSs are not merely
passive responses to the MJO but actively participate in its evolution. The findings provide an
observational basis for improving our conceptual understanding of multiscale tropical convection
and its role in intraseasonal variability.
1. Introduction
The Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) is the dominant mode of tropical intraseasonal variability
and exerts strong influence on global weather and climate through extreme rainfall events and
tropical–extratropical teleconnections (Zhang 2005, 2013; Stan et al. 2017; Henderson et al. 2017).
Convection associated with the MJO is highly organized across a wide range of spatial and temporal
scales.
In particular, the MJO envelope typically contains multiple eastward- and westward-
propagating superclusters of cloudiness (Nakazawa 1988; Chen et al. 1996), within which numerous
mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) are embedded (Houze 2004). These MCSs are the primary
contributors to tropical rainfall, accounting for up to 50 percent of total precipitation in many
tropical regions (Tao and Moncrieff 2009).
While the modulation of MCS activity by large-scale MJO environments has been extensively
documented (Lin and Johnson 1996; Chen et al. 1996; LeMone et al. 1998), a key outstanding ques-
tion is how MCSs collectively feed back onto the MJO. In particular, the upscale impacts of MCSs
on the momentum and heat budgets of the MJO remain insufficiently quantified. This gap is critical
because current coarse-resolution global climate models often simulate poorly organized MJOs
characterized by weak or intermittent eastward propagation, unrealistic intraseasonal variability,
and weak westerly wind bursts (Jiang et al. 2015). Such deficiencies have been hypothesized to
arise from an inadequate representation of MCSs and their upscale effects.
3


In contrast, cloud-resolving and superparameterized models that explicitly or partially resolve
MCSs are able to reproduce key features of the MJO more realistically (Grabowski 2003; Miura
et al. 2007; Grabowski 2001; Randall et al. 2003; Majda 2007a; Xing et al. 2009). This contrast
highlights the importance of representing MCS-scale processes and motivates the development of
physically based parameterizations of their collective effects.
Previous observational and theoretical studies have shown that MCSs can significantly influence
large-scale dynamics through convective momentum transport. Organized convection can produce
mesoscale fluxes that differ fundamentally from those associated with isolated convective towers,
including countergradient momentum transport that can enhance vertical shear (Moncrieff 1981,
1992; LeMone 1983; LeMone and Moncrieff 1994; Zhang and McFarlane 1995). Within the MJO,
such convective momentum transport has been shown to vary systematically with phase, including
downgradient behavior in some regimes and upgradient transport during westerly wind phases
(Tung and Yanai 2002a,b; Oh et al. 2015). Furthermore, embedded MCSs may play an active role
in organizing large-scale convection and promoting MJO propagation (Grabowski and Moncrieff
2001).
From a theoretical perspective, multiscale asymptotic frameworks have demonstrated how or-
ganized convection can influence planetary-scale dynamics through eddy momentum and heat
transport (Majda 2007b; Brenowitz et al. 2018). Idealized and mesoscale theories further suggest
that MCS-scale convective momentum transport can interact with convectively coupled waves and
background shear to modulate large-scale circulation (Majda and Stechmann 2009; Khouider et al.
2012; Yang and Majda 2018b,a). These results emphasize the potential importance of upscale
MCS impacts in shaping MJO dynamics.
Despite this progress, most existing studies focus either on idealized models or on localized
process-level analysis.
A comprehensive observational diagnosis of the two-way interactions
between the MJO and MCS populations remains limited. In particular, how MCS activity system-
atically varies with MJO phase, and how aggregated MCS activity feeds back onto the large-scale
MJO circulation in observations, are still not fully quantified.
In this study, we address this gap by using satellite-based MJO indices together with a long-term
objectively tracked MCS dataset. We systematically examine the modulation of MCS properties by
the MJO and diagnose the corresponding large-scale circulation anomalies associated with MCS
4


activity. By analyzing these coupled relationships across MJO phases, we aim to quantify the
two-way feedback mechanisms between the MJO and MCSs from an observational perspective and
to provide a clearer picture of their multiscale interaction.
2. Methodology
We use observational datasets to independently characterize the evolution of the Madden Julian
Oscillation and mesoscale convective systems and then examine their statistical relationships.
The MJO is identified using a standard real time multivariate MJO index based on large scale
circulation and outgoing longwave radiation anomalies, which provides a phase based description
of its propagation and amplitude. MCSs are tracked using a satellite based infrared brightness
temperature tracking algorithm that objectively identifies convective clusters and follows their life
cycles in time and space. This dataset provides information on MCS frequency, intensity, and
spatial organization across the tropics.
To quantify MJO MCS interactions, we construct phase composites of MCS properties as a
function of MJO phase and amplitude, including MCS occurrence, precipitation characteristics,
and spatial distribution. We further examine associated large scale circulation and thermodynamic
anomalies conditioned on MCS activity to assess the feedback from aggregated MCS populations
onto the MJO environment. All analyses are performed on daily to intraseasonal time scales,
with filtering applied to isolate variability associated with the MJO. This framework provides a
consistent observational basis for diagnosing two way statistical relationships between the MJO
and MCSs.
3. Result
We first examine the large scale structure and phase evolution of the Madden Julian Oscillation
using composite analysis of the MJO index. As shown in Fig. 1, the MJO exhibits a clear eastward
propagating signal characterized by alternating regions of enhanced and suppressed convection.
The horizontal structure evolves systematically across phases, with convective anomalies initiating
over the Indian Ocean and propagating into the Maritime Continent and western Pacific. The
accompanying circulation fields show coherent transitions in zonal wind and moisture convergence,
consistent with the canonical view of the MJO as a coupled convective dynamical system. The

We next quantify the contribution of mesoscale convective systems to total MJO precipitation.
Figure 2 shows that MCSs account for a dominant fraction of tropical precipitation within the MJO
envelope. This fraction is not constant but varies systematically with MJO phase, reaching its
maximum during active convective phases and decreasing substantially during suppressed phases.
This result indicates that the MJO does not merely modulate total precipitation but also reorganizes
the relative importance of organized mesoscale systems within the convective spectrum.
The
enhanced contribution of MCSs during active phases suggests that organized convection becomes
the primary rainfall mode when large scale environmental conditions are favorable, reinforcing the
hierarchical nature of tropical convection.
To further explore this modulation, Fig. 3 compares key MCS characteristics between active and
suppressed MJO phases. A robust contrast is evident across multiple metrics. MCS frequency
increases markedly during active phases, indicating more frequent initiation of organized convective

Figure 4 provides a spatial perspective on these differences by showing the horizontal distribution
of MCS frequency anomalies between active and suppressed MJO phases. The pattern reveals a
coherent large scale structure, with enhanced MCS activity concentrated within the convectively
active region of the MJO and suppressed activity in surrounding regions. This dipole like structure
highlights the role of the MJO as a large scale organizing agent that selectively enhances mesoscale
convective development in specific longitudinal sectors. The spatial coherence of these anomalies
further suggests that MCS modulation is tightly linked to the propagating MJO circulation rather
than being purely local.
Finally, Fig. 5 extends the analysis to a broader set of MCS properties, including lifetime duration,
cold cloud shield area, total precipitation, and propagation speed. All variables show consistent
enhancement during active MJO phases across large regions of the tropics, particularly over the

4. Concluding Discussion
This study provides an observationally based assessment of the two way feedback mechanisms
between the Madden Julian Oscillation and mesoscale convective systems. By combining a phase
resolved MJO framework with an objectively tracked long term MCS dataset, we document how
convection is organized across scales and how mesoscale systems both respond to and actively
shape intraseasonal variability.
The results demonstrate a clear hierarchical organization of tropical convection within the MJO
envelope. The MJO systematically modulates MCS activity, controlling their frequency, intensity,
spatial distribution, and structural properties. Active MJO phases are characterized by significantly
enhanced MCS occurrence and more organized convective systems, while suppressed phases
exhibit reduced and weaker mesoscale activity. Importantly, MCSs contribute a substantial and
phase dependent fraction of total tropical precipitation, indicating that they are not simply embedded
features but a dominant component of the MJO precipitation budget.
9


Beyond this downward control, the analysis also provides observational evidence for an upward
feedback from MCS populations to the MJO scale circulation. Spatially coherent anomalies in
MCS activity are aligned with the MJO convective envelope and exhibit organized large scale
patterns consistent with their potential to reinforce intraseasonal variability through aggregated
effects. The modulation of MCS properties, including duration, size, precipitation, and propagation
characteristics, further suggests that MCSs actively participate in regulating the effective structure
and evolution of the MJO.
Together, these findings support a conceptual framework in which the MJO and MCSs form
a coupled multiscale system rather than a one way hierarchical cascade. The MJO provides the
slowly varying environment that organizes mesoscale convection, while the collective behavior of
MCSs contributes back to the maintenance and modulation of the MJO circulation. This two way
interaction emphasizes that accurate representation of tropical intraseasonal variability requires
understanding not only how large scale dynamics controls convection, but also how organized
mesoscale convection feeds back onto planetary scale variability.
